title: Samson's last prayer (Judges 16:23–30)
hook: blind and shackled, the strong man prays one more time

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gideon's three hundred, and your line was less is enough. What did you start with only what you had? Day seven hundred six.

"Call for Samson, that he may make us sport." That's a crowd at a feast. The lords of the Philistines have gathered at the temple of their god Dagon to celebrate, and they say their god has delivered their enemy into their hand. The enemy is Samson, the strong man of Israel: betrayed by Delilah, his hair shaved, his eyes put out, bound with fetters of brass and set to grinding at the mill in the prison house. Now they bring him out to amuse them. A boy leads him by the hand. The text says about three thousand men and women are on the roof alone, watching. And there's one small line, a few verses back, that the reader knows and the crowd doesn't.
screen: `A BOY LEADS HIM BY THE HAND.`

segments.voice: Here's the line, verse twenty-two: "Howbeit the hair of his head began to grow again after he was shaven." Samson asks the boy to let him feel the pillars the house stands on. Then he prays. In the King James Bible: "O Lord GOD, remember me, I pray thee, and strengthen me, I pray thee, only this once, O God, that I may be at once avenged of the Philistines for my two eyes." It's worth hearing honestly. This is not a gentle prayer. Samson asks for revenge, for his eyes. Some readers sum up his whole story that way: strong, impulsive, careless with the vow over his life. And yet the text keeps this prayer, and the prayer is answered. Look at the first words, though, before the anger: remember me. He doesn't open with his rights or his record. He asks to be remembered. And only this once. He seems to know he has no credit left. Then: "Let me die with the Philistines." He bows himself with all his might, the pillars give way, and the house falls on the lords and on the people. The chapter closes with a grim tally: those he killed at his death were more than those he killed in his life. Readers don't agree on how to hear this ending. Some hear a sacrifice. Some hear a tragedy, a man whose strength was never matched by wisdom. Centuries later, Hebrews chapter eleven reaches him in a hurry. The writer runs out of room and starts listing names: "the time would fail me to tell of Gedeon, and of Barak, and of Samson." No verdict, no story, just the name, set beside the man from the winepress. Some readers say that's enough. At the very end, blind, shackled and mocked, he still knew whom to call.

Here's the practice: speak from your weakest place. Settle, and breathe. Let your attention go to a place where you're not strong right now: something you've lost, a mistake you keep paying for, a part of your life that feels shackled. Don't dress it up. Samson didn't. If you pray, you can borrow the first words of his prayer, only those: remember me. Say them, and stop. If you don't pray, simply hold that weak place gently, the way you'd hold someone else's, and breathe. Nothing needs fixing in two minutes. The bell holds the time.
Samson's last prayer. Blind and shackled in the temple of Dagon, the strong man asks: remember me, and strengthen me, only this once.
Your line: remember me, just this once. Today, ask for help with the weak thing you named, from God or from a person, in one plain sentence. Day seven hundred six.

howItsDone: Christians read Samson's story in more than one way, as a warning about strength without wisdom and as a sign that a prayer from the lowest place is still heard, and some point out that Hebrews 11:32 still lists his name.

original.note: Hebrew: remember me, the first request of Samson's prayer in Judges 16:28.

trapdoor: what you thought: Samson, a superhero with magic hair.
what it means: a careless strong man, blinded and mocked, whose last prayer begins remember me.
what a scholar hears: zochreni, remember me (Judges 16:28), in a prayer for vengeance the text doesn't clean up, and Hebrews 11:32 still lists him.

notes: 'About three thousand men and women' on the roof is from Judges 16:27.
'Careless with the vow over his life' and 'careless with what he was given' summarize the earlier Samson chapters (13:5 Nazirite vow; 14–16); interpretive. Confirm the tone is fair.
The prayer for vengeance is presented honestly, with two readings of the ending (sacrifice; tragedy) offered without ranking. The closing 'he still knew whom to call' is attributed to 'some readers'.
The practice offers only the real words 'remember me' from Judges 16:28 for those who pray; no new prayer is written.
